A.explanation: The unloading curve meets the strain axis at a positive strain when stress is zero, so there is permanent deformation and the behaviour is plastic, not purely elastic.

B.explanation: The unloading curve returns to the origin where both stress and strain are zero, so there is no permanent strain and the material is purely elastic.

C.explanation: The unloading is a vertical drop at constant strain to zero stress, leaving a large residual strain, so the deformation is permanent and plastic.

D.explanation: The unloading curve does not return exactly to the origin but to a small positive strain, so a small permanent deformation remains.

hints: Look at where each unloading curve finishes when stress returns to zero on the stress-strain axes.
Recall that purely elastic means zero strain when the stress is removed, so the unloading curve must return to the origin.
Compare graphs A, C and D, which finish at positive strain, with the one graph where loading and unloading both start and end at $0$.
walkthrough: Identify the test for purely elastic behaviour: after loading to a strain and then unloading to zero stress, the strain must also return to zero with no permanent set.
Check graph A: the unloading arrow reaches the strain axis to the right of $0$, so at zero stress strain $> 0$. This is permanent deformation.
Check graph C: unloading drops vertically at almost constant strain, so at zero stress a large strain remains. This is permanent plastic deformation.
Check graph D: the straight loading and unloading lines form a narrow loop that meets the strain axis at a small positive strain, so a small permanent set remains.
Check the remaining graph: loading and unloading form a loop that starts at $0$ and returns to $0$, so zero stress corresponds to zero strain with no residual extension. This is option B.
